source_text: Igitur si constat a quo persecutio eventiat, possumus iam consultationem tuam inducere et determinare ex hoc ipso praetractatu fugiendum in persecutione non esse. Si enim persecutio a deo evenit, nullo modo fugiendum erit, quod a deo evenit; sicut duplex ratio defendit, quia neque debeat devitari neque possit evadi quod a deo evenit. Non debet devitari, quia bonum; necesse est enim bonum esse omne quod deo visum est. Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est, Et vidit deus quia bonum est, non quod ignoraret bonum esse, nisi vidisset, sed ut hoc sono portenderet bonum esse quod deo visum est? Multa quidem sunt, quae a deo eveniant et alicuius malo eveniant. Immo bonum est ideo, quia a deo evenit, ut divinum, rationale. Quid enim divinum non rationale, non bonum? Quid bonum non divinum? Si autem sensui cuiusque videtur, non sensus hominis praeiudicat statui rerum, sed status sensui. Status enim unusquisque certum quid est et dat sensui legem ita sentiendi statum sicuti est. Si autem statu quidem bonum quod a deo venit (nihil enim a deo non bonum, quia divinum, quia rationale), sensui vero malum videtur, erit status in tuto, sensus in vitio. Statu optima res pudicitia et veritas et iustitia, quae a multorum sensu displicent. Numquid ideo status sensui addicitur? Ita et persecutio statu bona est, quia divina et rationalis dispositio, sensui eorum vero, quorum malo venit, displicet. Vides etiam illud malum rationale apud deum habere, cum quis in persecutione evertitur de salute, sicut et bonum illud ratione contingere, cum quis ex persecutione proficit in salute, Nisi si irrationaliter quis aut perit apud dominum aut salvus est, is non poterit persecutionem malum dicere, quae etiam in mali parte bonum est, dum ratione administratur. Ita si bonum persecutio quoquo modo, quia de statu constat, merito definimus quod bonum est vitari non oportere, quia delictum sit quod bonum est recusare, eo amplius, quod deo visum est, iam vero nec posse vitari, quia a deo evenit, cuius voluntas non poterit evadi. Igitur qui putant fugiendum aut malum exprobrant deo, si persecutionem uti malum fugiunt (bonum enim nemo devitat), aut fortiores se deo existimant, qui putant se evadere posse, si deus tale aliquid voluerit evenire.
thought_title: Persecution is from God, therefore good and unavoidable
orientation: Tertullian is answering Fabius's question about flight, arguing from the premise just established that persecution comes from God.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if it is established from whom persecution comes, we can now introduce your consultation and determine from this very preliminary treatment that there must be no flight in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, in no way will there be need to flee what comes from God; as a double reasoning defends, because what comes from God neither ought to be avoided nor can be escaped. It ought not to be avoided, because it is good; for it is necessary that everything which has seemed good to God be good. And surely it was not for this reason that it was written in Genesis thus, 'And God saw that it was good,' not that he would not have known that it was good unless he had seen it, but so that by this sound he might indicate that what has seemed good to God is good? Many things indeed are, which come from God and come for someone's harm. Rather it is good for this reason, because it comes from God, as divine, as rational. For what divine thing is not rational, not good? What good thing is not divine? But if it seems otherwise to anyone's perception, the perception of man does not prejudge the status of things, but the status prejudges the perception. For each status is something certain and gives to perception the law of perceiving the status just as it is. But if by status indeed what comes from God is good (for nothing from God is not good, because divine, because rational), but to perception it seems evil, the status will be in safety, the perception in fault. By status the best things are chastity and truth and justice, which displease the perception of many. Surely the status is not for that reason made subject to perception? So also persecution is good by status, because it is a divine and rational arrangement, but it displeases the perception of those for whose harm it comes. You see also that that evil has a rational basis with God, when someone in persecution is overturned from salvation, just as that good happens by reason, when someone from persecution advances in salvation. Unless if someone either perishes before the Lord or is saved irrationally, that person will not be able to call persecution evil, which even in the part of evil is good, while it is administered by reason. Thus if persecution is good in whatever way, because it is established from status, we rightly determine that what is good ought not to be avoided, because it would be a sin to refuse what is good, all the more because it has seemed good to God; and now indeed it cannot be avoided, because it comes from God, whose will will not be able to be escaped. Therefore those who think there must be flight either reproach God with evil, if they flee persecution as evil (for no one avoids what is good), or they consider themselves stronger than God, who think that they can escape, if God has willed such a thing to happen.

choices.english: that there must be no flight in persecution
choices.why: The gerundive fugiendum expresses necessity; 'flight' is the glossary term for fuga, and the negation non esse applies to the whole necessity.
rejected: that one should not flee in persecution
that fleeing in persecution is not necessary

choices.why: evenit means 'comes about' or 'happens'; the phrase is repeated as a refrain, and 'comes from God' preserves the source emphasis.
status here means the fixed, objective condition or standing of a thing; 'status' is kept as a technical term to preserve Tertullian's contrast with sensus (perception).
sensus here is the subjective human perception or judgment, contrasted with objective status; 'perception' captures the subjective faculty.
dispositio means an ordered plan or arrangement; 'arrangement' preserves the sense of divine ordering.
exprobro takes a dative of person and accusative of thing; 'reproach God with evil' preserves the construction and the accusation.

bible_refs.note: Et vidit deus quia bonum est

pass_b_english: So if it is established from whom persecution comes, I can now take up your question and settle it from this very preliminary discussion: there must be no flight in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, then in no way must there be flight from what comes from God. A twofold argument defends this: what comes from God should not be avoided, and it cannot be escaped.

It should not be avoided, because it is good. For everything that has seemed good to God must necessarily be good. And was it not for this reason that Genesis says, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:31)—not because he would not have known it was good unless he had seen it, but to indicate by this expression that what has seemed good to God is good? Many things, to be sure, come from God and come for someone's harm. No—it is good precisely because it comes from God, as something divine and rational. For what is divine that is not rational, not good? What is good that is not divine?

But if it seems otherwise to anyone's perception, human perception does not prejudge the status of things; rather, the status prejudges perception. For each thing's status is something fixed, and it gives perception the law of perceiving that status as it is. If, then, by status what comes from God is good—for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine, because it is rational—but to perception it seems evil, the status will be secure, and the perception at fault. By status, chastity, truth, and justice are the best things, yet they displease the perception of many. Does that mean the status is made subject to perception? So too persecution is good by status, because it is a divine and rational arrangement, but it displeases the perception of those for whose harm it comes.

You see that even that evil has a rational purpose with God, when someone is overturned from salvation in persecution, just as that good also comes about by reason, when someone advances in salvation through persecution. Unless someone perishes before the Lord or is saved irrationally, he will not be able to call persecution evil, since even in its harmful part it is good, as long as it is administered by reason.

So if persecution is good in whatever way, because it is established by status, we rightly determine that what is good ought not to be avoided, because it is a sin to refuse what is good—all the more so when it has seemed good to God. And further, it cannot be avoided, because it comes from God, whose will cannot be escaped. Therefore those who think there must be flight either reproach God with evil, if they flee persecution as an evil—for no one avoids what is good—or they consider themselves stronger than God, if they think they can escape when God has willed such a thing to come about.

problems.source_quote: Et vidit deus quia bonum est
problems.why: The Latin alludes to Genesis 1:31, not 1:10.
problems.ruling: Phrase 'Et vidit deus quia bonum est' recurs in Genesis 1; 1:31 is the specific verse, not 1:10.

fixed: Changed Genesis 1:10 to Genesis 1:31: the Latin 'Et vidit deus quia bonum est' alludes to Genesis 1:31, where God saw everything he had made and it was very good.

problems.quote: For each thing's status is something fixed, and it gives perception the law of perceiving the status as it is.
problems.why: Circular and word-for-word; the philosophical point about status preceding perception is lost.
problems.fix: Simplify: 'each thing's nature is fixed, and perception must conform to it.'

edits.old: For each thing's status is something fixed, and it gives perception the law of perceiving the status as it is.
edits.new: For each thing's status is something fixed, and it gives perception the law of perceiving that status as it is.

fixed: The English is close to the source but slightly awkward; the source 'dat sensui legem ita sentiendi statum sicuti est' means the status gives perception the law of perceiving the status just as it is. The edit removes the slight circularity by making the object of perceiving clearly the status, not the perception itself.

polish.changed: Clarified the philosophical argument about status and perception by breaking up dense sentences, making the logical progression explicit, and ensuring each pronoun and referent is clear for a modern reader.
